article.headline: The Terminal as Protocol: smux Bridges Competing AI Coding Agents
article.lede: Getting AI agents from different vendors to collaborate has been, until recently, a problem requiring formal plumbing: bespoke adapters, shared schemas, agreed-upon protocols. Shawn Pana, a developer from San Diego, noticed a shortcut: every major AI coding agent already knows how to run a shell command, and the terminal already knows how to multiplex. His tool, **smux**, makes the terminal window itself the message bus.
article.body:
The multi-agent coordination problem, stated plainly: Claude Code (built by Anthropic) and Codex (built by OpenAI) come from competing vendors with no shared protocol layer. Getting them to hand work to each other would ordinarily require one or both to implement a standardized interface — an *MCP* (Model Context Protocol) adapter for tool access, or an *A2A* (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) arrangement involving structured task-delegation schemas and discoverable “agent cards.” Both approaches add overhead; neither is designed for ad-hoc cross-vendor pairing on a local developer workstation.

smux sidesteps the whole stack. At its core is a shell utility called *tmux-bridge*, which any tool capable of running bash can invoke. Agents use it to read another agent’s *terminal pane* output, send labeled messages stamped with the sender’s identity and pane address, or relay keystrokes. The “protocol,” such as it is, is free-text *POSIX terminal I/O* — no schemas, no handshakes, no coordination between Anthropic and OpenAI required. A safety constraint enforces a read-before-act cycle: an agent must observe a pane’s current state before it can write to it, preventing blind message injection.

The elegance lies in what agents already know how to do. Claude Code and Codex both execute shell commands as a core capability; smux requires no new runtime, no server, and no integration work from either vendor. A developer installs it with a single curl command, labels their *tmux* panes, and can set one agent to draft code while a second reviews it — each reading the other’s output without human copy-paste. The repo crossed **1,400 GitHub stars** within days of the demo tweet, amplified by AI-practitioner audiences including AlphaSignal.

The approach has real limits. Terminal output scrolls away; messages are untyped free-text rather than validated schemas; the whole system depends on tmux running as the container. It will not scale to distributed or cloud-hosted agent fleets, and it offers none of the error-handling guarantees of a formal protocol. What it provides instead is zero integration cost and a human-readable audit trail: every inter-agent exchange is visible in the pane scrollback, interruptible by a developer at any moment. For local development workflows, that is frequently the right trade.

concepts.definition: Anthropic’s open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources via structured HTTP and JSON schemas. Designed primarily for tool access — databases, APIs, file systems — rather than peer-to-peer agent communication.

Google’s open protocol for structured communication between AI agents. Agents advertise their capabilities via discoverable JSON files called “agent cards,” then exchange structured task-delegation messages. Each participating agent must explicitly implement the protocol.

A terminal multiplexer — a program that lets a single terminal window host multiple independent shell sessions, each in its own pane or window. Developers use it to run several processes side by side; smux builds on tmux’s native pane-addressing and I/O-capture capabilities.

The shell CLI at the core of smux. It wraps standard tmux commands into agent-friendly operations: listing panes, reading their output, typing labeled messages, and sending control keys. Any process that can invoke bash can use it without additional dependencies.

A subdivided region within a tmux session, each running its own independent shell or process. Panes can be split horizontally or vertically, addressed by numeric ID, and assigned human-readable labels via tmux-bridge.

The text-based input/output standard governing how programs read from and write to terminal devices on Unix-like systems. Because it predates any AI agent framework, it is a universal lowest-common-denominator interface that every command-line tool already speaks.

In the A2A protocol, JSON files that an AI agent publishes to advertise its capabilities, accepted input formats, and communication endpoints — analogous to a business card for machine-to-machine discovery.

repos.summary: smux is a tmux configuration layer and shell utility (tmux-bridge) that gives AI agents the ability to read, write to, and send keystrokes across terminal panes. It is designed to let agents from different vendors communicate by treating the terminal as a shared message bus, with no network server or custom protocol required. The repo includes a SKILL.md file written for AI agents explaining how to use tmux-bridge as a tool, making it self-documenting for its own target audience.
